body: Hello. For about ninety days, a gentle note each day will keep you company as you move on from a friendship that has ended, and help you open up to the friendships ahead.
The end of a friendship can hurt as much as a break-up, yet there are fewer words for it. Your sadness is valid.
Today, simply name what you have lost: the person, the routine, the shared jokes, the sense of being known.
Friendships end for many reasons: distance, change, conflict, or simply growing apart. Not every ending is someone's fault.
Write down one good memory from the friendship. Endings do not erase what was real and kind.
You may keep reaching for your phone to tell them something. That reflex fades with time, slowly.
Notice the stories you tell yourself about why it ended. Are they kind to you? Are they fair to them?
It is fine to grieve someone who is still alive. The relationship is what you are mourning.
Talk to one person who knows you well about how you are feeling. You do not have to keep this quiet.
Resist the urge to check their social media today. Each check reopens the wound a little.
If you feel anger, let it be there without acting on it. Anger often protects deeper hurt.
Look after the basics today: food, water, sleep, a little fresh air. Grief of any kind is tiring.
Mutual friends can make things awkward. You do not have to explain everything to everyone.
Write a letter to your old friend that you will not send. Say what you never got to say.
If you think you made mistakes, note what you have learned. Growth does not require punishing yourself.
If they hurt you, you are allowed to protect yourself from further hurt, even if you still care about them.
Notice the space this friendship used to fill. You do not need to fill it immediately.
Some friendships are meant for a season. Letting one end can be a sign of growth for both of you.
Spend time today with someone who makes you feel at ease.
If you feel tempted to reach out, wait a day and ask what you hope will happen. Then decide.
You are not unlovable because one friendship ended. You are someone who has loved and lost, like everyone.
Remove or archive old photos and messages if seeing them hurts. You can always look at them later.
Notice which parts of the friendship you miss and which you do not. Both lists are informative.
Plan one small activity this week that you used to do with them, alone or with someone else. Reclaim it.
If you feel embarrassed about how it ended, remember most people have had a friendship fall apart.
Make a list of qualities you value most in a friend. It will help you recognise good friends in the future.
Be patient with your feelings. Some days you will feel fine and others it will sting again.
Notice when you replay old conversations. Gently bring yourself back to the present.
Reach out to a friend you have neglected while this friendship took up space.
If you see your old friend by chance, a polite hello is enough. You do not have to have a big conversation.
Ask yourself what you need now: comfort, distraction, understanding or closure. Seek that kindly.
It is fine to feel relief as well as sadness. Some endings bring both.
Try a new activity where you might meet people who share your interests.
Notice the urge to defend yourself to mutual friends. Let your kindness speak for you instead.
Write down three things you are proud of in how you treated people in that friendship.
The end of one friendship can make you cautious. That is understandable, and openness will return.
Remember that you can still wish someone well while not wanting them in your life.
Spend a little time on a project or hobby that belongs only to you.
If the ending was sudden, you may never get an explanation. You can create your own sense of closure.
Notice how much lighter some days feel compared with the first weeks.
Talk to a counsellor or trusted adviser if the loss is affecting your daily life. Help is a strength.
Halfway through. Take a moment to notice the small ways you have begun to heal.
Allow yourself to enjoy something today without thinking about the friendship.
If the friendship was long, you may have changed together. Notice who you are now on your own.
Practise saying a simple sentence about the ending if people ask: We drifted apart, and I wish them well.
Consider whether there are patterns in your friendships you would like to change.
Spend time with people who make you laugh. Laughter is a reminder that joy is still available.
Notice the kindness you show yourself in this time. It will help in future friendships too.
If you share a group of friends, find ways to enjoy them without needing to avoid every gathering.
Write down what you would like future friendships to feel like.
Remember that you have made friends before, and you can do it again.
Say yes to one invitation this week, even if you feel unsure.
If you find yourself comparing new people to the old friend, notice it and let each person be themselves.
Notice how much more energy you have when you are not carrying the friendship's weight.
Allow some memories to become gentle rather than painful. Time helps this happen.
Be honest with new friends about what you need, early and kindly.
Notice any bitterness and ask whether it is serving you. You can put it down when you are ready.
Spend a day doing things that remind you of who you were before the friendship.
If they reach out, you can take time to decide how to respond. You do not owe an instant answer.
Remember that forgiveness, if you choose it, is for your peace, not their approval.
Write down one thing the friendship taught you about yourself.
Notice that you can hold both gratitude and hurt about the same person.
Invest in one friendship that has stood the test of time. Tell them you value them.
Reflect on how you might handle conflict differently in future friendships.
If a birthday or anniversary of the friendship comes round, plan something comforting for that day.
Notice the friend you were in that friendship. Keep the parts of yourself you liked.
If you feel lonely, reach out to one person and suggest a simple plan.
Notice how you are rebuilding a social life that fits who you are now.
Let go of one possession or habit that keeps the old friendship too present.
Remember that endings make room for new beginnings, even if you cannot see them yet.
Try a group activity or class this month, somewhere friendships can grow naturally.
Notice who has shown up for you during this time. Thank them.
If you wonder whether you should try to repair the friendship, ask whether both of you want that.
Spend time outdoors today, letting your mind rest from overthinking.
Remember that your worth does not depend on any one relationship.
Notice how much more you understand about what you need from friendships now.
Write a short note to your future self about what you have learned.
Allow yourself to feel proud for getting through a hard and lonely kind of loss.
If old feelings resurface, greet them as visitors rather than as signs you have not healed.
Notice any new friendships that are beginning to form, however small.
Keep the practices that helped: talking to others, limiting social media, writing it down.
Remember that you are someone who can love deeply and also let go when needed.
Look back at your list of qualities you value in a friend. Who already shows them?
Celebrate the friendships that are still in your life. They are worth your attention.
You may always miss parts of the friendship, and that is fine. Missing is a sign it mattered.
Think about how you want to show up for the friends you have now.
Look back over these weeks. What helped you most to move on?
Notice how far you have come from the first raw days.
Remember that you can return to these thoughts whenever a friendship changes in the future.
Keep your heart open to new people, even if you are a little more careful now.
You started by naming what you lost. Now you know what you want to build.
This is the last note. You have moved through the end of a friendship with care, and you are ready for the friendships still ahead.
